item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees could make a surprising decision on veteran infielder Ryan McMahon before the playoffs.
New York clinched a playoff berth. They will likely be in the Wild Card series again, likely playing the Boston Red Sox for the second year in a row.
The Yankees are 88-64.
New York Yankees Could Bench Ryan McMahon
With the Yankees heading back to the playoffs, New York could have to make a difficult decision on veteran infielder Ryan McMahon.
McMahon is a solid glove-first third baseman, but he has struggled offensively since coming to New York. With that, Yankees analyst Pat Ragazzo of FanSided believes New York could remove McMahon from its playoff roster, or simply have him on the bench.
"Should Rosario's hot streak continue into the end of the regular season, the Yankees find a way to utilize him at third base during the postseason," Ragazzo wrote. "There's even a world where Jose Caballero slides to third, with Anthony Volpe available off the bench. McMahon will probably still get a roster spot, but they cannot play his bat regularly in the biggest games of the year. McMahon's bat creates a black hole in the Yankees' lineup, which they cannot afford to deploy in October.
"If not for his defense, McMahon would've likely been designated for assignment by now. And given his historically poor offensive numbers, it seems like it could be headed that way with McMahon under contract for another year at $16 million. The 31-year-old just has not worked out as a member of the Yankees. His time in pinstripes should come to an end sooner rather than later."
McMahon has one more year on his six-year, $70 million deal. Not having him on the playoff roster would be a tough look. Yet, his bat has struggled, and the Yankees could use Caballero at third, with Volpe as the primary backup infielder in the playoffs.
McMahon is hitting .210 with 10 home runs and 34 RBIs this season.
New York Right Now
The Yankees have clinched a playoff spot and once again have World Series aspirations.
Although New York did clinch a playoff spot, the Yankees know the job is not done.
"Every year you go through a lot, it seems like. But we've been through a lot this year with injuries, with adversity," Yankees manager Aaron Boone said. "But credit to them for coming together. Through all the ups and downs, they've been a together group. I feel like they've developed a lot of grit over the season."
The Yankees are set to begin a three-game road series against the Arizona Diamondbacks on Friday.

item.title: [Stadium Rant] #13 Jazz Chisholm Jr's New York Sweet Honeymoon Tune Is Tuning Down After The 2026 Season
item.dc:creator: Natalie Robinson

item.content:encoded:
Jazz Chisholm Jr. is one of the most electrifying MLB players around. From his charisma, high energy, confidence, and million-dollar smile, he’s made it clear that being in pinstripes has brought his love for baseball back. His future with the New York Yankees could become one of the biggest questions of the 2026 offseason. The two-time All-Star is scheduled to reach free agency after the season, leaving his future in the Bronx uncertain.
Chisholm has never blended into the background. Since his MLB debut, he has electrified fans with his charismatic personality, bold style, and, most importantly, his explosive play on the field. As the 2026 season draws to a close, all eyes are on this Bahamian superstar —not just for his highlight-reel moments, but for what his future will hold after his 2026 season with the New York Yankees.
Jazz Chisholm Jr.’s Early Career And Rise To MLB Stardom
Chisholm’s journey to the major leagues is a story of perseverance and raw talent. His passion for baseball was evident from an early age. In 2015, he signed with the Arizona Diamondbacks as an international free agent. Showcasing his natural skills, speed, and infectious energy, he caught the attention of the Miami Marlins and made his MLB debut in 2020.
After making his debut, Jazz wasted no time making an impact and electrifying fans. Since his rookie season, he has showcased his potential with his speed and power. His skills did not go unnoticed, earning him an All-Star selection in 2022 and establishing him as one of the game’s most exciting young stars.
The Yankees Era: Highs, Lows, And Star Power
After leaving the Marlins, Chisholm found a renewed sense of happiness when the Yankees acquired him in a blockbuster trade ahead of the 2025 season. They hoped his dynamic skill set would energize their lineup. Once he made it to the Bronx, he immediately brought the fire and flair to the game. His bat speed, base-stealing prowess, and defensive versatility at both second base and center field made him a valuable asset.
Despite the highs, lows, and injuries, Chisholm has made an incredible impact in New York. From his acrobatic plays on the field, clutch home runs in key games, to his swagger and the love from the fans, it is understandable how being in the Bronx gave him back his happiness.
Will Jazz Chisholm Jr. Stay With The Yankees In 2027?
As the 2026 season progressed, rumors began circulating about the Yankees’ roster plans. According to Heavy, recent reports have raised questions about whether the Yankees will bring Chisholm back for 2027. Disappointing to many fans, this development is not entirely surprising. The Yankees are reportedly looking to invest in pitching and have several top prospects ready to debut in the infield and outfield.
If the Yankees ultimately decide not to bring Chisholm back, his time in the Bronx would end after just two seasons. While it marks the end of an era, it also opens the door to new opportunities. His unique skill set, marketability, and ability to energize a franchise make him one of the most sought-after free agents this winter.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. 2026 Yankees Stats
Chisholm may be sidelined at the moment; however, he managed to secure the following stats as a Yankee:
| Stat | 2026 |
|---|---|
| Batting average | .232 |
| Home runs | 19 |
| RBI | 55 |
| Stolen bases | 40 |
| OPS | .719 |
What’s Next For Jazz Chisholm Jr.?
Where will Chisholm go from here? With Chisholm approaching free agency, his future in New York remains uncertain but remains bright. Teams across Major League Baseball value his combination of athleticism, power, and charisma. Whether he lands with a contending team looking for a final piece or a rebuilding franchise seeking a new face, Chisholm’s next chapter promises to be just as exciting as his journey thus far.
End Of My Jazz Chisholm Jr. Rant
Now that the Yankees have punched their way into the postseason, this will be Chisholm’s last chance to make the best of it in New York and try to win a World Series. His career is a testament to rising above expectations and seizing the moment. As the 2026 season concludes, fans and analysts will closely watch his next move, ensuring his star continues to shine brightly in baseball. So I ask the fans: what do you think? Do you think Jazz Chisholm Jr. will remain in New York for 2027, or will the Yankees decide it’s time to move in a different direction?

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees' Latest Austin Wells Update Won't Shock Anyone
item.dc:creator: Matthew Schmidt
item.description: Austin Wells has been a massive liability offensively for the New York Yankees this season, but they have not seemed to care. item.content:encoded:
Austin Wells has been a massive liability offensively for the New York Yankees this season, but they have not seemed to care.
The Yankees didn't heavily pursue a catcher at the MLB trade deadline, and it's looking more and more like they will head into 2027 with Wells behind the plate.
Not that that should surprise anyone based on how New York has handled the situation.
Chris Kirschner of The Athletic provided an update on Wells in a recent mailbag, revealing that while the Yankees may try and pursue a platoon bat to pair with Wells this winter, they probably won't make any major changes at catcher.
"Austin Wells is one of the best defenders behind the plate. The Yankees' pitchers fully trust him, and he's a major reason they've had success this season," Kirschner wrote. "Clearly, his offense has nosedived this year. It's frankly shocking. The Yankees will likely be in the market for a platoon partner for Wells for next season. Catching fewer games than he did this year could keep his legs fresher."
Is it really that shocking, though?
Wells slashed .219/.275/.436 last season. Yes, he flashed some pop with 21 home runs, but when he wasn't running into a pitch for a homer, he was barely getting on base.
This year, he is slashing .179/.277/.313. Funny enough, his on-base percentage is actually better than last year thanks to his improved walk rate, but his power (12 home runs and .135 ISO) has declined significantly.
Wells owns a lifetime .212/.289/.392 slash line. He has never been a force offensively. Sure, he calls a good game and he is fine behind the dish, but the idea that Wells is Pudge Rodriguez defensively is pretty ridiculous.
Keeping Wells is fine. He would be a terrific backup. But retaining him as the starter with his .590 OPS this season would be criminal. That's especially considering Ryan Jeffers will be available in free agency.
But as Kirschner noted, the most likely scenario is that the Yankees will try and find a right-handed backstop to alternate with Wells.
The first name that comes to mind in that regard is Tyler Stephenson, who is a far superior hitter to Wells. The problem? Stephenson has actually hit righties (.760 OPS) better than lefties (.701 OPS) throughout his career.
No matter what direction New York proceeds this offseason, it will likely end in Wells remaining the starting catcher.

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — La diferencia de tres puntos de Cody Bellinger en el platoon le da a los Yankees una gran ventaja en la alineación para la postemporada de octubre.
Con un balance de 88-64, los Yankees ya se han asegurado una plaza en la postemporada, pero siguen a cinco partidos de los Tampa Bay Rays en la División Este de la Liga Americana, cuando quedan 10 partidos de la temporada regular. La clasificación sigue siendo importante. Y también lo es una alineación que tendrá poco margen de error cuando los rivales puedan adaptar sus estrategias de pitcheo para contrarrestarla.
Ahí es donde la postemporada de 2024 sigue siendo un contexto útil. Nueva York llegó a la Serie Mundial antes de caer ante los Dodgers en cinco partidos, pero el jardín izquierdo nunca llegó a ser una fuente fiable de producción tanto ofensiva como defensiva. Alex Verdugo terminó esa temporada regular con un promedio de .233/.291/.356 y un OPS+ de 83, y luego bateó .208/.309/.313 con un OPS de .622 en 14 partidos de postemporada.
El problema duró más de un mes de octubre. Tras la última temporada de Brett Gardner con los Yankees en 2021, el jardín izquierdo pasó a ser una posición rotativa en lugar de un punto fuerte consolidado. Las estadísticas posicionales de FanGraphs sitúan al jardín izquierdo de los Yankees en solo 1,6 fWAR entre 2021 y 2024, lo que lo coloca en el puesto 28 de las Grandes Ligas en ese periodo. Esa trayectoria dejó a Nueva York buscando tanto rendimiento como estabilidad, en lugar de otro parche de una sola temporada en una posición defensiva clave. Por fin, la situación parece haber cambiado.
Bellinger convierte el jardín izquierdo de un compromiso en un punto fuerte
Cody Bellinger es la razón más clara. El miércoles conectó 3 de 5, con una base por bolas, una carrera y una base robada, lo que le ha permitido sumar varios hits en cinco de sus últimos siete partidos. Su racha va más allá de unas cuantas noches de septiembre.
Bellinger ha bateado .340 con cinco jonrones, 18 carreras impulsadas y un wRC+ de 148 en 23 partidos desde que volvió el 23 de agosto tras una distensión de grado 2 en el isquiotibial izquierdo. Al comenzar el viernes, llevaba un promedio de bateo de .276/.351/.444, con 16 jonrones y 71 carreras impulsadas en 125 partidos.
Los Yankees acabaron con un balance de 15-7 en los primeros 22 partidos tras su regreso, batearon .274/.336/.440 como equipo, registraron un diferencial de carreras de +42 y anotaron al menos cinco carreras en 14 ocasiones. Llegaron a las seis carreras en 12 ocasiones y a las siete en nueve. Bellinger ha aportado toda esa potencia ofensiva sin dejar de ser un defensor decisivo.
Sports Info Solutions le atribuye a Bellinger 20 carreras defensivas salvadas en el jardín izquierdo, mientras que Statcast le da seis outs por encima de la media en todo el jardín. Ese valor en ambos aspectos es la diferencia clave con respecto a 2024, y su capacidad para jugar tanto en el jardín central como en primera base aporta a los Yankees una mayor flexibilidad en la plantilla.
Una derrota aplastante dejó claro por qué su bate es tan importante
Los Yankees pudieron comprobar su poder ofensivo durante la derrota por 12-2 ante los Mets el 12 de septiembre en el Yankee Stadium. Bellinger anotó las dos carreras de Nueva York con un sencillo impulsador en la cuarta entrada y un jonrón solitario en la sexta. Era su tercer jonrón en cuatro partidos en ese momento.
Aaron Boone estaba explicando por qué el lanzador titular de los Mets, Zac Thornton, había controlado al resto de la alineación. Ese comentario ponía de manifiesto lo poco que Cody Bellinger había recibido ayuda aquella tarde.
«Está claro que se puso por delante ahí y sus lanzamientos a la zona de strike fueron realmente buenos», dijo Boone.
Desde entonces, el promedio de bateo de Bellinger en septiembre ha subido hasta el 0,390 en 14 partidos, con cuatro jonrones, 12 carreras impulsadas y 14 carreras anotadas. Los Yankees han necesitado esa estabilidad mientras otras partes de la alineación han tenido que adaptarse a las lesiones y a los enfrentamientos.
Una diferencia de tres puntos en el platoon cambia las cuentas de octubre
Quizá la cifra más reveladora sea la que apenas varía. Hasta el miércoles, Bellinger tiene un OPS de 0,797 contra lanzadores zurdos y un OPS de 0,794 contra lanzadores diestros. Esa diferencia de tres puntos le da a los Yankees un bateador en el centro del orden de bateo que no hace falta ocultar cuando los rivales cambian de lanzador.
El panorama del platooning de los Yankees también sitúa a Aaron Judge y Ben Rice entre sus bateadores titulares más equilibrados. Bellinger es otro bateador que puede quedarse en el partido sin que Boone tenga que sacrificar el ataque por la defensa ni la defensa por el ataque, una cualidad muy valiosa cuando, en octubre, los bullpens cambian los enfrentamientos inning tras inning.
El precio original del traspaso solo cuenta la mitad de la historia
Los Yankees ficharon a Bellinger de los Cubs en diciembre de 2024 a cambio del lanzador diestro Cody Poteet, y Chicago también aportó 5 millones de dólares. El precio de ese traspaso sigue siendo impresionante, pero no es el coste total. Después de que Bellinger se convirtiera en agente libre, Nueva York lo volvió a fichar en enero con un contrato de cinco años y 162,5 millones de dólares.
En 2025, sumó 29 jonrones, 98 carreras impulsadas y 4,9 fWAR. El valor que le da FanGraphs para 2026 ronda ahora los cuatro fWAR. Según un cálculo basado en sus estadísticas totales de la MLB durante las dos temporadas con los Yankees , se sitúa en 45 jonrones, 169 carreras impulsadas y un promedio de bateo combinado de aproximadamente .274/.341/.464.
Con la clasificación para la postemporada asegurada y la División Este de la Liga Americana aún en juego, a los Yankees les quedan 10 partidos para pulir su alineación de octubre. El reciente repunte de Bellinger, su rendimiento casi idéntico en el plato y su defensa en el jardín izquierdo aportan a Nueva York algo que su equipo de la Serie Mundial de 2024 nunca tuvo de forma constante en esa posición: un titular que puede seguir formando parte del plan independientemente del rival.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario más abajo.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Los Yankees se han pasado todo el mes de septiembre intentando convertir su clasificación para la postemporada en una plantilla más clara de cara a octubre. Una de sus decisiones más difíciles de tomar ahora mismo tiene que ver con la tercera base.
Ryan McMahon llegó como un jugador que aportaba estabilidad sobre todo en defensa, pero cada vez le cuesta más ocultar su bateo. Su último bache se produjo el miércoles en el Target Field, donde se fue de 0 de 6 con cuatro strikeouts en la derrota por 5-4, en 13 entradas, ante los Minnesota Twins.
Los Yankees no dejaron de remontar. Anthony Volpe empató el partido con un doble en la novena entrada. Ali Sánchez puso a Nueva York por delante en la décima, y José Caballero sumó un fly de sacrificio en la undécima. Minnesota respondió en cada ocasión hasta que Víctor Caratini sentenció el partido con un sencillo decisivo en la 13.ª. Tommy Nance se llevó la victoria, John Schreiber la derrota y no hubo salvamento.
McMahon, que bateaba séptimo, terminó la noche con un promedio de .210/.275/.346, 10 jonrones y 34 carreras impulsadas en 118 partidos. Se ha puesto a cero 101 veces, lo que supone un porcentaje del 29,2 %, mientras que su OPS es de .621. Las estadísticas avanzadas actuales que acompañan a las críticas le sitúan en un wRC+ de 77 y un fWAR de 0,5.
Este momento hace que cada turno al bate sin resultado se note más. Los Yankees llegaban al viernes con un balance de 88-64, a cinco partidos de Tampa Bay en la División Este de la Liga Americana, con la clasificación para la postemporada ya asegurada. Jazz Chisholm Jr. sigue en la lista de lesionados de 10 días por un esguince en el pulgar derecho, mientras que Volpe ha vuelto de la Triple A y ha jugado como segunda base.
La trayectoria de Volpe en las ligas menores ha ampliado las opciones de los Yankees. Durante su etapa en la Triple A, jugó como shortstop, segunda base y tercera base. Eso no significa que sea la solución definitiva para la tercera base, pero le da a Aaron Boone otra opción de alineación que tener en cuenta cuando vuelva Chisholm.
McMahon también tiene un sueldo garantizado de 16 millones de dólares para 2027. Los Yankees tienen que decidir si su defensa y su contrato siguen justificando que sea titular cuando la diferencia en ataque se ha vuelto tan grande.
McMahon entra en la zona de peligro de LeMahieu
Esa combinación ha hecho que cada vez más gente de los Yankees se plantee una pregunta más dura: si McMahon debería perder su puesto de titular, quedar fuera de la plantilla de la postemporada o, al final, ser designado para cesión.
La comparación que está cobrando fuerza es la de DJ LeMahieu, a quien los Yankees dejaron libre en julio de 2025 cuando aún le quedaban por cobrar unos 22 millones de dólares. Según FanGraphs, en su última temporada con los Yankees, LeMahieu registró un wRC+ de 94, un porcentaje de embasado de 0,338 y una tasa de strikeouts del 24,6 %.
McMahon está por debajo de todos esos indicadores ofensivos. Su porcentaje de llegada a base de 0,275 y su tasa de strikeouts del 29,2 % hacen que los Yankees obtengan menos aportación ofensiva de la que recibían de LeMahieu antes de decidir que ya no encajaba en su plantilla.
Las situaciones no son iguales. LeMahieu tenía 36 años, su papel se había reducido y Nueva York quería a Chisholm en segunda base. McMahon es más joven y sigue aportando valor en tercera base. Pero la decisión sobre LeMahieu dejó claro que el dinero garantizado no siempre protege el puesto de un veterano en la plantilla.
Boone sigue centrándose en el grupo
Los Yankees no han dicho públicamente que McMahon vaya a quedar fuera de la plantilla. Tras asegurarse el título, Boone habló de cómo el vestuario había afrontado una temporada difícil, en lugar de dar a entender que se hubiera tomado ninguna decisión sobre un veterano.
«Pero hay que reconocerles el mérito de haberse mantenido unidos. A pesar de todos los altibajos, han sido un grupo muy unido», dijo Boone.
Ese comentario no aclara cuál será el papel de McMahon en octubre. Lo que sí hace es resaltar la diferencia entre las presiones externas para que lo echen y la decisión que los Yankees hayan tomado realmente.
La defensa ya no es la respuesta definitiva
El argumento más sólido de McMahon sigue siendo su guante. La instantánea que te he pasado muestra un DRS de -1 y un Fielding Run Value de +1, mientras que la página en directo de Statcast muestra un valor defensivo global ligeramente positivo. La cifra exacta varía según la métrica y el momento de la actualización, pero la ventaja defensiva no oculta un OPS de 0,621.
Un tercera base con un OPS de 0,621 puede seguir siendo una opción válida si su defensa es de primera y el resto de la alineación está en forma. Los Yankees tienen menos margen mientras Chisholm esté de baja, y en octubre cada puesto de la alineación cobra más importancia.
Volpe no es un tercera base contrastado en las Grandes Ligas, y los Yankees no han dado a entender que tengan pensado darle esa posición. Aun así, su reciente actuación en esa posición en la Triple A le da a Boone una alternativa real. Su experiencia como campocorto hace que la objeción sobre la potencia de su brazo no sea tan sencilla, pero eso no garantiza que vaya a defender bien la tercera base en octubre.
La comparación de Okamoto hay que ponerla en contexto
Otra comparación que circula entre los aficionados de los Yankees compara a McMahon con el tercera base de Toronto, Kazuma Okamoto. Según la MLB, Okamoto tiene un promedio de bateo de 0,235, con 33 jonrones, 88 carreras impulsadas y un OPS de 0,774. Su contrato de cuatro años y 60 millones de dólares tiene un valor medio anual de 15 millones de dólares.
McMahon gana 16 millones de dólares y lleva 10 jonrones con un OPS de 0,621. A primera vista, el contraste es enorme.
No se trata de una decisión de la directiva en la que se pueda comparar a uno con otro sin más. McMahon ya tenía contrato cuando los Yankees lo ficharon en 2025, mientras que Okamoto llegó a la MLB siguiendo un camino diferente como agente libre. Aun así, la comparación salarial ayuda a entender por qué se han intensificado las críticas y por qué algunas de ellas se han extendido hasta el director general, Brian Cashman.
Octubre obliga a los Yankees a decidirse por un papel
No hay indicios confirmados de que los Yankees hayan decidido designar a McMahon para cesión o sacarlo de la plantilla de la postemporada. Sigue en activo, y la incertidumbre sobre la fecha de regreso de Chisholm hace que la situación en el cuadro siga siendo incierta.
Pero la cuestión ya no es si McMahon está pasando por una mala racha. Es cuánto tiempo de juego pueden permitirse los Yankees darle a un bateador con un wRC+ de 77 cuando empiece octubre.
Nueva York comienza este viernes una serie de tres partidos en el Chase Field contra Arizona. McMahon tiene tiempo para cambiar el rumbo, pero los Yankees ahora tienen menos margen de maniobra y más alternativas en el cuadro que hace un mes.
¿Qué te parece? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Gerrit Cole has a Yankees start that matters more than it looks
item.dc:creator: Alexander Wilson
item.description: Friday night in Arizona is not a playoff game. Gerrit Cole does not need to turn it into one. But the Yankees are 88-64, they have already punched their postseason ticket, and their next start gives them something September rarely offers: a chance to watch their ace work without the standings screaming at every pitch. Cole is listed to face Eduardo Rodriguez in the opener of the Diamondbacks series. For me, the useful part is not whether he gets the win. I want to see Gerrit Cole work through a
item.content:encoded:
Friday night in Arizona is not a playoff game. Gerrit Cole does not need to turn it into one.
But the Yankees are 88-64, they have already punched their postseason ticket, and their next start gives them something September rarely offers: a chance to watch their ace work without the standings screaming at every pitch. Cole is listed to face Eduardo Rodriguez in the opener of the Diamondbacks series.
For me, the useful part is not whether he gets the win. I want to see Gerrit Cole work through a settled routine.
The Yankees need the boring version of this start
Cole does not have to rack up 10 strikeouts or carry a no-hitter into the seventh. The Yankees need crisp work, clean recovery between innings, and the kind of outing that makes a manager's postseason decisions less complicated.
That may sound less fun than a big velocity reading or a gaudy line, but this is where the club is. There is no prize for treating every September start like a referendum. The value is getting Cole through a normal workload and having him leave Arizona feeling like he has another ordinary start coming.
Arizona is a better check than it seems
The Diamondbacks are 80-73 and still playing for something. A road game at 9:40 p.m. Eastern against a capable opponent is not a controlled tune-up, either. It will ask for the normal concentration, pitch execution, and in-game adjustment that October will demand.
I would not overreact to one rough inning, especially with the schedule nearly finished. I also would not dismiss a sharp one. The Yankees have enough arms and enough moving parts that every clean Cole outing gives the club one less thing to worry about when the games finally tighten up.
0What do you think?Post a comment.
Cole's line will matter. His rhythm will matter more.

However, in spite of the victory, the team dealt with a notable injury out of their bullpen to right-handed reliever Jonathan Bowlan, who has been a workhorse for the Phillies this year. item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies opened a series with the New York Mets on Thursday night and won the game 3-0 to improve to 85-68 overall.
However, in spite of the victory, the team dealt with a notable injury out of their bullpen to right-handed reliever Jonathan Bowlan, who has been a workhorse for the Phillies this year.
He exited the eighth inning after recording two strikeouts with a reported groin strain.
Don Mattingly Makes Honest Statement on Injury
While it’s still unknown exactly the extent of the injury and how long Bowlan may be out, Phillies interim manager Don Mattingly made an honest statement after losing a key arm out of the pen.
“Paul said right groin tightness, so we’ll reevaluate tomorrow to see where he’s at,” Mattingly said. “We’ll talk about it more tomorrow but at this point you just… I don’t want to be cold hearted but you got to move on and you have to find a way to fill that spot. Which is not necessarily easy to do, but that means other guys got to step up, that’s all.”
“That means other guys got to step up, that’s all.”
Don Mattingly says other arms will need to rise to the occasion if Jonathan Bowlan misses time. pic.twitter.com/5FnoNJ2Mjv
— NBC Sports Philadelphia (@NBCSPhilly) September 18, 2026
Bowlan’s 2026 Season
In his fourth MLB season, but first with the Phillies after spending the last three years with the Kansas City Royals, Bowlan has been one of the best arms out of Philadelphia’s pen.
He’s appeared in 59 games, and across 56.1 innings pitched, he holds a 2-2 record with a 3.36 ERA, 73 strikeouts, and two saves.
Looking at the Phillies
Philadelphia is still trying to chase the Atlanta Braves in the NL East, trailing them by 4.0 games with nine regular-season games remaining.
The Phillies also want the top Wild Card spot, which would give them home-field advantage in a best-of-three Wild Card Series, but they remain tied with the Chicago Cubs for that spot.

item.title: [MLB.com] Schlittler, Rice more than just most valuable Yanks, they're indispensable
item.dc:creator: Mike Lupica
item.description: The two most valuable Yankees this season are a starting pitcher named Cam Schlittler, from Walpole, Mass., and Northeastern University, a school within walking distance of Fenway Park, and Ben Rice, who comes out of Cohasset, Mass., on the state’s South Shore, about 30 miles from Fenway. If the Yankees are hosting a Wild Card Series against the Red Sox in less than two weeks -- at Yankee Stadium and not Fenway -- Schlittler and Rice will be the biggest reasons. Schlittler ought to win the AL Cy
item.content:encoded:
The two most valuable Yankees this season are a starting pitcher named Cam Schlittler, from Walpole, Mass., and Northeastern University, a school within walking distance of Fenway Park, and Ben Rice, who comes out of Cohasset, Mass., on the state’s South Shore, about 30 miles from Fenway. If the Yankees are hosting a Wild Card Series against the Red Sox in less than two weeks -- at Yankee Stadium and not Fenway -- Schlittler and Rice will be the biggest reasons.
Schlittler ought to win the AL Cy Young Award and ought to be an MVP candidate for the whole league. David Cone, now a Yankees broadcaster for the YES network and once a great Yankee himself, has one word to describe what he’s seen from Schlittler this season:
“Nails.”
Here’s a breakdown of Schlittler’s ERA, month by month after one start in March, when, of course, he threw a shutout (eight strikeouts) into the sixth inning against the Giants:
1.73 in April
1.48 in May
3.38 in June
1.93 in July
2.33 in August
0.86 so far in September
Carlos Rodón got hurt. Max Fried got hurt. Gerrit Cole joined the season late, and he hasn’t looked like his own Cy Young self lately. It is been Schlittler who has been the Yankees' ace, who is their Game 1 guy, who has carried the staff. He is not going to end up with a 25-3 record and an ERA of 1.74 the way Ron Guidry did nearly 50 years ago. But Schlittler is at 14-6 with a 1.95 ERA going into his last few starts of the regular season. He has been the first young power starter out of the Yankees’ system since Guidry to be this good, and this dominant.
But Rice has been just as important to their offense.
In a season when Aaron Judge was gone for more than 80 games because of a fracture to his rib cage. Then, after Judge finally got back into the lineup and even hit his first home run in months, he left a game against the Twins the other day because of pain in his lower leg. It is why you have to believe, if and when Judge is back in the lineup again, he’s going to be a swing and a prayer the rest of the way.
So No. 99 went away. So did Cody Bellinger, the Yankees’ second-most important hitter a year ago, before he finally returned from the IL. But even when the Yankees struggled to score runs, and even in a roller-coaster year that saw Rice hit just .196 in June and .184 in August, it is Rice who has been the Yankees' hitting star, coming into a weekend series against the Diamondbacks with 38 home runs and still with a chance to knock in 100.
Luis García Jr. showed up from the Nationals at the Trade Deadline to give him some backup. Bellinger has been on a heater since coming off the IL, with five homers, 18 RBIs and a .344 average over his last 22 games. But it was Rice around whom the Yankees built what offense they had before all that, while they were staying ahead of the Red Sox and at least maintaining contact with the Rays.
You know how many homegrown Yankees have hit 40 or more home runs in a season in the last 75 years? Two. One was named Mickey Mantle and the other is Judge. There have been other Yankees sluggers who got to 40 and beyond. Alex Rodriguez once made it all the way to 57. But they all came from somewhere else. Rice is the same as Schlittler: He hasn’t just come to this moment from New England, he’s someone the Yankees drafted in the 12th round of the 2021 Draft (Schlittler was out of the seventh round the following year).
Alfonso Soriano made his own run at 40 more than 20 years ago. Did it twice. But Soriano came to the Yankees as a free agent from Japan. So think about the company Rice will be keeping if does get to 40 homers, starting with his chance this weekend against the Diamondbacks:
Mantle. Judge.
Here is something Rice’s manager, Aaron Boone, has said about him:
"I got my first taste of him in Spring Training of '24, and it was like, 'Oh, OK.' But then this year, it's gone to even another level.”
Here is something else:
“I think he's turning into one of the best hitters in the league."
Rice himself has predictably low-keyed what he’s done for the Yankees so far.
"The year is still in progress, you know?” he said. “It's still going on. We've got more games to play and a long road ahead, so I can't really look back and assess it fully yet."
It really has been a roller-coaster ride occasionally. He has struggled occasionally against left-handed pitchers, but his season-long average against them stands at .254 with 10 home runs and 29 RBIs.
We know what Schlittler’s numbers are. Rice’s, though, can get a little lost sometimes. But in a year where he’s batted everywhere from leadoff to cleanup, when Judge was gone for more than half the time, he has been indispensable, too. And still has a shot to be a 40-homer guy for the Yankees.

item.content:encoded:
Why it's 'hard to argue' against Spencer Jones in Yankees center field battle originally appeared on The Sporting News. Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
The New York Yankees appear to be locked in as the AL's first Wild Card seed.
With just a trio of regular season series remaining, the Yankees and their coaching staff/front office should be thinking about how they'll fill out the postseason roster.
One topic of discussion will almost certainly be who is starting in center field.
Bleacher Report's Kerry Miller believes it should be rookie Spencer Jones over the currently injured Trent Grisham.
"Though he hasn't come close to matching the 35 HR, 29 SB, .932 OPS line he posted in the minors in 2025, it's hard to argue with the .802 OPS he's posted since the beginning of June," Miller wrote about Jones. "Even if Grisham is healthy heading into October, Jones might be New York's primary CF in the postseason."
Jones stands out above Grisham for two reasons:
First, he's hitting .362 in 47 at-bats with runners in scoring position. That could be incredibly valuable for the Yankees in October.
Plus, Jones has more than proven that he can handle left-handers, hitting .435 with three home runs and 12 RBIs in 46 at-bats against southpaws.
Grisham's Grade 2 hamstring strain certainly complicates his return, given the Yankees probably want the freshest players on the field.
And Grisham regressed significantly on offense (.211/.308/.395, .703 OPS) after swatting 34 home runs with an .811 OPS in 2025.
Based on recent results and the health of the two players, Jones seems like the clear choice for manager Aaron Boone.

item.title: [Yardbarker] Yankees Make Cam Schlittler Announcement on Friday
item.dc:creator: Simeon Kotto
item.description: Some New York Yankees fans had been wondering if the team would start to limit Cam Schlittler’s innings or even potentially skip one of his remaining starts with the playoffs in view, but it doesn’t appear that the Yankees are planning on that. At least for now. The Yankees have locked in their starting pitchers for this weekend’s three-game series in Arizona, and the headline assignment is Schlittler taking the ball Saturday against the Diamondbacks, via MLB.com. item.content:encoded:
Some New York Yankees fans had been wondering if the team would start to limit Cam Schlittler’s innings or even potentially skip one of his remaining starts with the playoffs in view, but it doesn’t appear that the Yankees are planning on that. At least for now.
The Yankees have locked in their starting pitchers for this weekend’s three-game series in Arizona, and the headline assignment is Schlittler taking the ball Saturday against the Diamondbacks, via MLB.com.
With the club already in the postseason but still chasing both the American League East title and the top Wild Card seed, every start carries extra weight.
Manager Aaron Boone’s staff listed Gerrit Cole for Friday, Schlittler for Saturday, and Will Warren for Sunday, setting up a rotation that showcases the team’s depth heading into the final stretch.
Schlittler’s outing is the one that stands out. The right-hander has been the anchor of New York’s staff all year, posting a 14-6 record with a 1.95 ERA and 228 strikeouts.
Those numbers have made him the clear favorite for the American League Cy Young Award and, in the view of many around the league, the best pitcher in baseball this season … although he has already racked up 184.2 innings. He will face Arizona’s Brandon Pfaadt, who enters with a 7-3 mark and a 3.77 ERA.
The contrast is sharp: a dominant, high-strikeout ace against a solid but far less overwhelming counterpart.
The Yankees’ pitching staff as a whole has been exceptional. Their 3.19 team ERA ranks first in the majors, and they lead the league in fewest earned runs and runs allowed.
They have done it despite injuries that forced constant adjustments. Schlittler’s consistency has allowed Boone to manage the rest of the rotation with an eye toward October.
After this series, the club expects to have Max Fried and Carlos Rodón lined up for Tuesday’s doubleheader against the Tampa Bay Rays, with Cole and Schlittler available later in that set.
Sunday’s starter, Will Warren, has quietly put together a strong campaign of his own (10-6, 3.89 ERA). How Boone uses him in the postseason—whether as a fifth starter or a high-leverage reliever—will be one of the more interesting decisions of the coming weeks.
For now, the immediate focus is this weekend in the desert. Friday’s matchup pits Cole against Eduardo Rodriguez, Sunday features Warren opposite Corbin Burnes, and Saturday belongs to Schlittler.
The Yankees know the Diamondbacks can be dangerous at home, but they also know they possess one of the strongest rotations in the sport.
Giving the ball to Schlittler on Saturday is both a statement of confidence and a practical move. It also demonstrates that New York is not concerned about his workload.
If he continues to pitch the way he has all season, the Yanks will take another step toward securing home-field advantage and heading into October with its best possible alignment. The series begins Friday night. All eyes will be on Saturday.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Analyzing Where Clarke Schmidt May Fit into Yankees' Bullpen Trust Tree
item.dc:creator: Michael Zeno; Unknown
item.description: It wasn't all bad news from a discouraging and frustrating 13-inning defeat at the hands of the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday afternoon, even if it really, really stung for a number of reasons. The ray of sunshine in what was a rough day for the Yankees' divisional hopes was the return of someone they view as crucial to their chances at a deep playoff run. After a 440-day absence due to Tommy John surgery, Clarke Schmidt made his Yankees return, tossing two-thirds of an inning in the seventh befo
item.content:encoded:
It wasn't all bad news from a discouraging and frustrating 13-inning defeat at the hands of the Minnesota Twins on Wednesday afternoon, even if it really, really stung for a number of reasons.
The ray of sunshine in what was a rough day for the Yankees' divisional hopes was the return of someone they view as crucial to their chances at a deep playoff run. After a 440-day absence due to Tommy John surgery, Clarke Schmidt made his Yankees return, tossing two-thirds of an inning in the seventh before being removed due to pitch count.
It wasn't the cleanest outing, as he wasn't able to get through a full inning after throwing 24 pitches to four batters, but for someone on a big league mound for the first time in 14 months, you had to like what you saw, striking out a pair and only surrendering a pair of soft-hit singles.
The runway is rather short for the remainder of the season with just 10 games left, but Schmidt will likely see his way into four or so games down the stretch. That gives him a total of five outings to truly figure out where he can fit into a wide-open bullpen trust tree.
Clarke Schmidt's bullpen experience
Converting a full-time starter to the bullpen is not always as easy as it seems, but it's a transition the Yankees will have to make three times as we head into the postseason, with Ryan Weathers' likely return and Will Warren's place in the rotation. That said, Schmidt has a bit of an advantage.
Before becoming a full-time starter at the major-league level in 2023, Schmidt was used almost exclusively as a reliever in his brief big-league stints, most notably in 2022, when he posted a 3.12 ERA in 57.2 innings as part of a makeshift bullpen that got very good results. He didn't get himself high up the totem pole, but he pitched some important innings for the club.
His playoff experience as a reliever was unfortunately one to forget. He was saddled with a pair of losses, first in Game 3 of the ALDS after a squeaker by Oscar Gonzalez got through the infield for a walk-off single, and the second in Game 1 of the ALCS against the Houston Astros, where he allowed home runs to Yuli Gurriel and Chas McCormick in the sixth inning of what would be the start of a sweep.
He was supposed to be in the bullpen the following season, but a mountain of injuries forced him to step up in the rotation, starting what became a nightmarish 2023 season. Since then, Schmidt has made 63 appearances through his season-ending elbow surgery in 2025, all but one as a starter.
That's not in the cards for 2026, so what can he do to be useful for the Yankees in the playoffs?
Where Schmidt could fit into unstable bullpen
Schmidt adds a multi-inning righty option to a bullpen that has a lot of moving parts. He leaned hard on a cutter-slider combo on Wednesday, but also featured his sinker, four-seamer, and curveball. His velocity looked as firm as ever, something that could be enhanced but didn't need to hold back for 100 pitches.
The bullpen's premier multi-inning righty is Paul Blackburn, who relies on a ton of spin and movement in his profile, making him more volatile in games with shoddy command. He, along with closer David Bednar and lefty Brent Headrick, makes up the team's three highest-leverage arms, but it's wide open beneath them, particularly after Fernando Cruz's elbow injury.
John Schreiber has been effective as a righty specialist in a small sample, so he feels like the leader in the clubhouse as the team's sixth-inning arm, but he might not be playable in certain matchups due to his struggles against lefties. Tim Hill's overall struggles, even if he remains sharp against lefties, will also give pause. Michael Fulmer and Luis Gil haven't pitched enough to earn trust in leverage.
There are two ways that Schmidt can be deployed. One of which is as the team's right-handed bridge reliever, as sort of a "platoon" with Ryan Yarbrough (or Weathers, when he returns). Lineups with more right-handed hitters will fare significantly better against Weathers or Yarbrough if the team needs them to come into a big spot to provide some length to the back-end guys, so having a guy with the opposite hand who can fill that role is valuable.
But that role could be reserved for Warren, who's more stretched out than Schmidt and isn't at risk of being removed due to a long inning. I doubt Schmidt would be permitted to throw much more than 30 pitches in a game. That could lead the 30-year-old to be more in the Schreiber role as the sixth-inning guy, possibly pitching in higher leverage if needed due to overuse.
There are a lot of questions about Schmidt as we come down the stretch, but the important thing is that he's back and he's healthy. The more bullpen depth, the merrier.

item.content:encoded:
The Philadelphia Phillies are using their newest pitching addition to reshape their weekend plans as they push toward the postseason.
Phillies manager Don Mattingly confirmed that right-hander José Urquidy will be active for Friday's game and used in a bullpen game against the New York Mets. The move allows Philadelphia to keep top pitching prospect Andrew Painter on his normal schedule for Saturday.
Urquidy was claimed off waivers from the Chicago White Sox on Thursday. He gives the Phillies another option to cover innings while the pitching staff deals with the absence of Jesús Luzardo.
The Phillies also transferred right-hander Caleb Kilian to the 60-day injured list to clear a 40-man roster spot for Urquidy.
The 31-year-old has spent most of the season working in a long-relief role. He threw 22.2 innings for the White Sox, posting a 4.37 ERA, 15 strikeouts and a 1.19 WHIP.
Urquidy has also pitched for the Pittsburgh Pirates this season and owns a 4.08 ERA across his MLB career. He previously faced Philadelphia during the 2022 World Series with the Houston Astros.
Painter will now get the extra day before making his Saturday start. The rookie has made 23 appearances, including 21 starts, and has logged 115.1 innings with 100 strikeouts and 43 walks.
The results have been uneven, with Painter carrying a 5.54 ERA, but he showed what he can provide in his most recent outing. He allowed one run over five innings against the Atlanta Braves on Sept. 13.
The timing of the move is also important for Philadelphia's bullpen. Urquidy can absorb innings Friday and help keep high-leverage relievers such as Jhoan Duran from being overworked with the postseason approaching.
Urquidy will not be eligible for Philadelphia's postseason roster because he was acquired after the Sept. 1 deadline. His immediate value is giving Mattingly another arm to navigate the final games of the regular season.
The Phillies entered Friday trailing the Cubs (85-68) by a half-game for the top Wild Card position. With the regular season winding down, the club is clearly prioritizing pitching availability and keeping its key arms on schedule.

Over 19 seasons with the New York Yankees, Rivera established himself as the greates
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE: Baseball legend Mariano Rivera on Yankees '90s Dynasty, Core 4, pressure of playing in NYC and his new Mo's Hot Sauce appeared first on ClutchPoints. Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here.
When the ninth inning arrived in the Bronx, nothing was more intimidating for opposing hitters than Mariano Rivera jogging out of the bullpen with his iconic "Enter Sandman" entrance music playing. Over 19 seasons with the New York Yankees, Rivera established himself as the greatest closer of all time, retiring as MLB's career leader with 652 saves. The first player ever unanimously elected to the Baseball Hall of Fame, Rivera was at his best when the stakes were highest, helping anchor a Yankees dynasty that won five World Series championships during his career.
From his virtually unhittable cutter to his unmatched composure in October, Rivera became synonymous with dominance in the ninth inning. He recorded an MLB-record 42 postseason saves and a remarkable 0.70 ERA across 141 playoff innings, playing an integral role alongside Derek Jeter, Andy Pettitte, and Jorge Posada in a homegrown group that became known as the Yankees' "Core Four."
Baseball legend Mariano Rivera with ClutchPoints' Rob Lepelstat for an exclusive interview in the Bronx, NY – just minutes from Yankee Stadium, where Mo spent his entire 19-year MLB career with the Yankees
Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial)
More than a decade after throwing his final pitch, Rivera's impact continues to extend beyond the mound. The Yankees legend has entered the hot sauce business with Mo's Heat, his new hot sauce brand that gives Rivera an opportunity to bring his competitive mentality into a completely different arena while connecting with fans in a new way.
During an exclusive interview with ClutchPoints' Rob Lepelstat, Rivera discussed the inspiration behind Mo's Hot Sauce, revealed the mentality that allowed him to thrive in baseball's biggest moments, reflected on the Yankees' iconic 1990s dynasty and his relationship with the Core Four, opened up about playing alongside "The Captain" Derek Jeter, and shared his advice for today's Yankees as they attempt to bring a 28th World Series championship to the Bronx.
Mo's Hot Sauce
Baseball legend Mariano Rivera made a career out of bringing the heat in the ninth inning. Now, the legendary New York Yankees closer is doing it in a much different way.
Rivera has entered the hot sauce business with Mo's Hot Sauce, adding another venture to a résumé that already includes five World Series championships, a unanimous Baseball Hall of Fame induction, MLB's all-time saves record (652) and recognition as the greatest closer in the history of the sport.
Mariano is proud of his roots, which is why Mo's Heat features authentic Panamanian flavors, hand-selected habanero peppers, and all-natural ingredients from their 122-year-old hot sauce recipe.
It includes three flavors: The Sinker, The Curve and the signature sauce, The Cutter (of course!), named after Rivera's unhittable pitch.
The venture is about more than simply putting his famous name on a bottle. He explained the motivation behind Mo's Hot Sauce and why he believes the product can stand out in a crowded market.
"This product is something special for me, dear to my heart, so I'm happy that we could come up with this," Rivera described. "It's all what you put in there, you know? Besides the ingredients, you have to put love and passion in there, you know, commitment. And—and that's what we have done. You know, besides all the ingredients that are in there, all-natural, by the way, I mean, we're putting a lot of effort, a lot of passion, love, and commitment to make sure that the fans and people love this sauce. Not because Mariano, but because of the sauce."
From the Mo's Heat website: Made with highly selected habanero peppers and spices using a 122-year-old recipe, Mo's Heat hot sauces offer a unique flavor and aroma to enhance any meal. As an MLB pitcher, Mariano Rivera played every game for his home country, Panama. And he founded Mo's Heat to celebrate their flavor, character, and fire.
Fans can find out more information, including where to buy, pricing, and flavors, at https://mosheatsauces.com/.
The Closer Mentality
When the Yankees needed three outs to close out a game, there was nobody they trusted more than Rivera.
The numbers speak for themselves. Rivera finished his career as MLB's all-time saves leader with 652, but his dominance became even more pronounced when the lights were brightest. In 96 postseason appearances, Rivera recorded 42 saves while allowing just 11 earned runs, good for the lowest ERA in playoff history (0.70).
Yet Rivera's greatness wasn't simply the product of his famous cutter. His ability to remain calm in moments that could overwhelm even the best players became as much a part of his reputation as the pitch itself.
Rivera explained how he approached those pressure-packed situations and what allowed him to maintain the same mentality whether he was pitching in a regular-season game or trying to record the final outs of a World Series.
"I tried to simplify the game, I tried to simplify the way I pitch… If I can get you out in one pitch, I would try to do that. I wasn't afraid of contact."
That mindset helped Rivera become synonymous with the closer position and gave the Yankees an enormous advantage during their championship years: When No. 42 entered the game, everyone in the ballpark knew exactly what was coming — and hitters still struggled to stop it.
Rivera's Cutter
Few weapons in sports history carry the mythic status of Mariano Rivera's cut fastball. Thrown with effortless arm speed and late, violent movement, the pitch shattered hundreds of bats—and just as many opposing rallies—en route to a record 652 career saves, and five World Series rings.
Hitters across Major League Baseball spent nearly two decades studying tape, anticipating the pitch, and bracing for it, yet virtually none could solve it. Ironically, the most unhittable pitch in baseball history wasn't engineered in a lab or perfected through endless trial and error; it was a divine accident that Rivera discovered while trying to do the exact opposite.
Rivcera's cutter came out of the exact same arm slot and had the same visual spin as his standard fastball. Batters had only roughly 0.17 seconds to react and could not tell the difference until it was too late.
The ball traveled at up to 90–95 mph and would break sharply by up to 8 inches, usually in the final 10 feet before reaching the plate.
Rivera threw the cutter roughly 88% of the time later in his career, per MLB.com. Hitters knew it was coming for nearly two decades, yet they still could not hit it.
When asked about the origin of his signature weapon, the Hall of Fame closer reflected on how a frustrating bullpen session with pitching coach Mel Stottlemyre ultimately gave birth to baseball perfection.
"It was God-given for sure, because we were trying to stop it from moving… I told [Mel Stottlemyre], 'Hey man, whatever's gonna happen is gonna happen, because I have no control of this pitch, let's leave it.'
The rest is history.
The Yankees' 1990s Dynasty
The Yankees' championship run of the late 1990s remains one of the greatest stretches by any team in modern baseball history.
After winning the World Series in 1996, New York put together a historic 1998 season before completing a three-peat with championships in 1999 and 2000. Over a five-season span, the Yankees won four World Series titles and established a dynasty that has yet to be replicated in MLB since.
Rivera was there for all of it.
Before becoming the Yankees' closer, Rivera played a crucial setup role during the 1996 championship season. Once he took over the ninth inning, he became one of the foundational pieces of a team that seemingly expected to be playing deep into October every year.
Looking back on those teams, Rivera reflected on what made that group so successful and why the Yankees were able to consistently perform when the stakes were at their highest.
The championships featured countless memorable moments, but Rivera believes the culture surrounding those Yankees teams was just as important as the talent on the roster.
"There was a—a commitment and—and a passion and love with 25 players. Well, before was the—the owner, you know, Mr. George was amazing, and then uh the coaching staff that they put together, Joe and—and the rest of the play—the rest of the coaches. And then the players. You know, I mean, we were family, we were a team, we were family. And that makes a lot of difference. You know, we don't—we don't try to separate ourselves, we try to unify ourselves even tighter, tighter and tighter. And as results, we have four championships in five years."
The Core 4
As the Yankees continued winning, four homegrown players became constants in the Bronx: Rivera, Derek Jeter, Andy Pettitte, and Jorge Posada.
Eventually dubbed the "Core Four," the group came through the Yankees organization together before becoming central figures in one of the most successful eras in franchise history. Rivera, Jeter, Pettitte, and Posada were teammates for five World Series championships, with their careers becoming permanently intertwined in Yankees history.
What made the group unique wasn't simply its success. Each player filled a distinctly different role, yet all four shared the experience of growing from prospects into established stars while dealing with the expectations that came with playing in New York.
Rivera reflected on his relationship with Jeter, Pettitte, and Posada and what it meant to experience so much of his career alongside the same group of teammates.
"We're talking about family. We're not talking about teammates or players… We grew up together, coming from the minor league system all the way to the big leagues… We were just brainwashed: 'We need to win regardless.' It's not about second place, it's about winning the whole thing."
Years after their final game together, the Core Four remains synonymous with an era when October baseball in the Bronx felt almost inevitable.
The Captain, Derek Jeter
Within that Core Four, Rivera shared an especially remarkable journey with Derek Jeter.
Both made their MLB debuts in 1995. Neither could have known at the time that they would spend nearly two decades together and eventually become two of the most recognizable Yankees of their generation.
Jeter became the captain and face of the franchise. Rivera became the greatest closer in baseball history. Together, they were fixtures on five championship teams and experienced virtually everything the sport had to offer.
Their partnership also produced one of the most memorable moments of Rivera's final season. During his last appearance at Yankee Stadium in 2013, Jeter and Pettitte walked to the mound to remove an emotional Rivera from the game.
Rivera discussed what made Jeter such a special teammate and leader and what stood out about playing alongside him for so many years.
"Derek was the perfect captain because he had us… three players, teammates, that loved him and were willing to do whatever it takes to make him look good. He was the face, he had to be in the media talking about it, but we were all doing the job."
For all their individual accomplishments, their careers will forever be linked by what they accomplished together in pinstripes.
Rivera's Advice for Today's Yankees
More than a decade after Rivera threw his final pitch, the standard in the Bronx remains the same.
Winning games isn't enough. Making the postseason isn't enough. For the Yankees, success is ultimately measured in championships.
Rivera understands that pressure better than almost anyone. He experienced the expectations that came with wearing the pinstripes while playing for teams that didn't just reach October — they expected to win once they got there.
Today's Yankees face the challenge of creating their own championship legacy while playing under the weight of that history. Rivera offered his advice for the current roster and explained what it takes to succeed in New York when expectations are at their highest.
"They know the advice. It's just—just you have to push. You have to keep pushing and pushing and pushing to get it done, because I mean, this thing is not easy. People know that winning championships is not easy at all. So, we have the team, we have the players, so we just have to have the determination and the passion to get it done, you know? However, you have to get it done, you have to find a way to get it done, and that's what we're doing."
The names and faces have changed since Rivera's championship years, but the goal hasn't. For a franchise with 27 World Series titles, the winningest team in North American professional sports history, the expectation will always be to add another one.
—
Related: This bold Aaron Judge take may cause Yankees fans to raise eyebrows
Rob Lepelstat is an experienced sports media professional with over 7+ years in content creation, editorial, social media, reporting/interviewing, etc. His work has been featured in USA Today, Yahoo Sports, Bleacher Report, and more. Check out more of his interviews, including Jay-Z, Kareem Abdul-Jabbar, Lawrence Taylor, Ray Lewis, Derek Jeter, Ice Cube, "Dr. J" Julius Erving, Drew Brees, and Livvy Dunne here.

item.content:encoded:
The Arizona Diamondbacks will play just one more series at home before the end of the 2026 regular season, and it'll be a marquee matchup with the AL-contending New York Yankees in downtown Phoenix this weekend.
An air of festivity — and, perhaps, desperation — will fill Chase Field, as Arizona sits four games back of the San Diego Padres and their playoff spot heading into Friday night's matchup.
The Yankees have already clinched a playoff appearance at 88-64 on the year, but would need close to a miracle to catch the Tampa Bay Rays for the AL East. They'll be throwing out three tough starting pitchers this coming series.
The Diamondbacks, meanwhile, can't afford to keep dropping games with just nine left to play, following a brutal 2-1 series loss to the Miami Marlins.
Here's how you can catch the game one action between these two teams on Friday night.
How to watch Diamondbacks and Yankees game one
Despite the national relevance of the Yankees, and the playoff race the Diamondbacks find themselves in, Friday night's game — which is scheduled for a late 9:40 p.m. Eastern Time and 6:40 p.m. local Arizona time first pitch — will not be a nationally exclusive broadcast.
Arizona has had its fair share of those national telecasts, as have the Yankees. But this game will be available by traditional viewing options.
For fans of the Diamondbacks, the game will be broadcast as usual via D-backs.TV, or the MLB.TV out-of-market package for those not living in the Phoenix or New York markets.
For Yankees fans, the game will be carried by the Yankees Entertainment and Sports Network (YES), as normal.
For those seeking radio-listening options, the game will be broadcast to Diamondbacks fans via Arizona Sports 98.7 FM (English), as well as La Campesina 101.9 FM & 860 AM (Spanish). Yankees fans can tune in to WFAN 660/101.9 FM and WADO 1280.
Gerrit Cole vs Eduardo Rodriguez
Eduardo Rodriguez is exactly the starting pitcher the Diamondbacks would like to see on the mound for an important game. He's delivered to the tune of a 2.62 ERA and 15 wins all season long.
The Texas Rangers got to Rodriguez in his most recent start, however, picking up six runs on eight hits in 5.1 innings, though only three of those runs were earned due to some poor Arizona defense.
Gerrit Cole is having an uncharacteristically poor stretch. He's allowed a combined seven home runs in his last two starts and has an ERA north of 6.00 in September. He's still managed to post a strong 3.67 ERA in his return from Tommy John surgery this year, however.
An Arizona native, Alex D'Agostino is the Publisher and credentialed reporter for Arizona Diamondbacks On SI. He previously served as Deputy Editor for Arizona Diamondbacks and Arizona Cardinals On SI and covered both teams for FanSided. Alex also writes for PHNX Sports. Follow Alex on X/Twitter @AlexDagAZ.
Follow alexdagaz

item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK — La candidatura de Cam Schlittler al título de MVP ha reavivado una pregunta que es más antigua que la analítica, más antigua que la sala de vídeo. Incluso más antigua que la mayoría de los que ahora la debaten.
¿Qué significa realmente el valor? Un antiguo as de los Yankees ha vuelto a sacar a colación este debate esta semana, con un lanzador que casi nadie esperaba que entrara en la discusión.
La mayor parte del mundo del deporte se ha decantado por una división clara. Un trofeo para el mejor lanzador, otro para el mejor bateador. Los aficionados de los Yankees llevan más de una década viendo cómo los votantes se inclinan por esa opción.
¿Podrá Schlittler, de 25 años, romper con la tendencia?
Un experto nacional lo dejó muy claro. Analizó el panorama, dijo que la elección era obvia y señaló a un bateador potente de Houston. Según él, caso cerrado.
Pero alguien de los Yankees no estaba dispuesto a dejarlo zanjado tan fácilmente.
La primera temporada completa de Schlittler le ha valido el mejor promedio de carreras limpias permitidas (ERA) de todo el béisbol. David Cone, el exlanzador de los Yankees y actual comentarista, se mostró en desacuerdo con la idea de que el MVP de la Liga Americana sea pan comido. Su argumento no tenía que ver con las cifras, sino con la propia palabra.
Una fuente cercana dice que la elección es obvia
La crítica que recibió Cone vino de Ken Rosenthal, de The Athletic. En un vídeo que se publicó el 14 de septiembre, un día después de que Cam Schlittler lanzara seis entradas sin encajar ninguna carrera contra los Mets, Rosenthal reconoció los méritos del lanzador diestro antes de descartar su caso.
Rosenthal mencionó a Yordan Álvarez, de Houston, y a esa temporada ofensiva que los votantes suelen premiar, lo que contradice directamente el argumento de los Yankees. Álvarez llegaba a esta semana con un promedio de bateo de .310, 38 jonrones, 96 carreras impulsadas y un OPS de 1,016, mientras lucha por la Triple Corona de la Liga Americana.
«Yordan Álvarez, en mi opinión, parece la elección más obvia por lo que ha logrado en ataque», dijo Rosenthal.
Esa es la opinión generalizada. Y es precisamente la que Cone se propuso complicar.
Un grande de los Yankees le da un nuevo enfoque al tema
Cone defendió su postura en un programa del New York Post junto a Joel Sherman y Jon Heyman. En lugar de discutir las estadísticas, volvió a la prueba más antigua que ofrece el premio: la de la sustracción. ¿Qué pierde un equipo sin un jugador?
Cone planteó el ejercicio en general. Preguntó dónde estarían los Royals sin Bobby Witt Jr., dónde estarían los Astros sin Álvarez y dónde estarían los Yankees sin su as. En su opinión, eso situaba a Schlittler al mismo nivel que los bateadores.
«Si este año no contaran con Schlittler en los Yankees, ¿dónde estarían?», preguntó Cone. «Schlittler está entre los mejores. Sin duda, merece que se le tenga muy en cuenta».
Es un argumento de peso, teniendo en cuenta la temporada que han tenido los Yankees. Aaron Judge solo jugó 65 partidos por culpa de una lesión, y Gerrit Cole, Max Fried y Carlos Rodón también se perdieron partidos. En medio de toda esa agitación, Schlittler fue la constante al frente de la rotación, un lanzador titular en su primer año que llevó al equipo a luchar por el título.
El dato que le mantiene en la carrera
Este es el detalle que mantiene vivo el argumento de Cone, y que pocos medios han destacado. Bradford Doolittle, de ESPN, elabora un índice global llamado AXE, y en su análisis de premios de septiembre situó a Schlittler en segundo lugar entre todos los candidatos al MVP de la Liga Americana. Álvarez lideraba la clasificación con 146,9. Schlittler le seguía de cerca con 143,0.
No es una diferencia abismal. Es un empate casi perfecto en un modelo diseñado para combinar el lanzamiento y el bateo en una sola cifra, y mantiene al as de los Yankees en la lucha. Doolittle seguía diciendo que era una tarea difícil.
Las cifras lo explican todo. Doolittle describió una sucesión de acontecimientos casi perfecta. Schlittler probablemente necesitaría al menos una salida más, seguramente una larga en la que no encajara ninguna carrera, para hacerse con el título de mejor promedio de carreras limpias permitidas de las Grandes Ligas en solitario, en lugar de solo liderar la Liga Americana.
Ni siquiera un final impecable bastaría por sí solo. Álvarez también tendría que quedarse sin la Triple Corona mientras los Astros no se clasifican para los playoffs, y Junior Caminero, de Tampa Bay, necesitaría tener una última semana pésima que hiciera perder a los Rays el liderato de la División Este de la Liga Americana. Es una situación casi imposible, y por eso llama tanto la atención que Doolittle esté dispuesto a incluir a Schlittler en su clasificación.
Unas estadísticas que dan que hablar
Las cifras que lo acompañan explican por qué se le menciona. Schlittler tiene un balance de 14-6, con una ERA de 1,95, 228 strikeouts, un WHIP de 0,90 y un bWAR de 7,1 en 31 partidos como titular. Su marca de 1,95 le empata con Jacob Misiorowski, de Milwaukee, en la mejor ERA de la liga.
El contexto de los récords es aún más impresionante. Las 21 salidas de Schlittler en las que solo ha cedido una carrera o ninguna suponen un récord de los Yankees en una sola temporada, según Sarah Langs, de MLB.com. No se trata solo de un mes brillante. Son siete meses de control casi total por parte de un lanzador novato.
Últimamente ha estado aún mejor, con una ERA de 0,86 este mes, mientras supera las 180 entradas. Varios medios lo sitúan como líder de la Liga Americana en WAR de Baseball-Reference, la métrica exacta que mide el valor que describió Cone. Su ERA también se encuentra entre las más bajas de un lanzador titular de los Yankees desde el 1,74 de Ron Guidry en 1978.
Una votación que gira en torno a una definición
La historia pone de relieve lo que está en juego. Justin Verlander, en 2011, fue el último lanzador a tiempo completo en ganar el MVP de la Liga Americana, y Clayton Kershaw, en 2014, fue el último lanzador en ganarlo en cualquiera de las dos ligas. Ningún lanzador a tiempo completo de los Yankees ha conseguido el premio desde Spud Chandler en 1943.
Por eso este tira y afloja va más allá de un solo nombre. Rosenthal valora el rendimiento a través de los resultados. Cone lo valora a través de la ausencia. Ambos puntos de vista son defendibles, y ninguna votación resolverá cuál es el correcto.
Los Yankees, con la mirada puesta en octubre, preferirían que su as reservara lo mejor de sí mismo para la postemporada, independientemente de los trofeos. Pero, con una o dos salidas por delante, Schlittler todavía tiene margen para dar un empujoncito al debate. Por ahora, el tema sigue abierto, y un grande de los Yankees insiste en que la pregunta más antigua de este deporte aún merece una respuesta.
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

item.title: [Pinstripe Alley] New York Yankees vs. Arizona Diamondbacks: Series Preview
item.dc:creator: Nick Power

item.content:encoded:
The Yankees squandered a chance to sweep the Twins Wednesday, dropping a 13-inning gut punch that diminished their chances of catching up to the Rays in the AL East. They’ll head to Phoenix this weekend for a three-game set against the Diamondbacks, who’ve dropped consecutive series and are hanging by a thread in the NL Wild Card race. With a four-game set against the Rays looming next week, this series against Arizona will be crucial in determining if the Yankees control their own destiny heading into the season’s final week. Let’s take a look at the likely starting pitching matchups.
Friday: Gerrit Cole vs. Eduardo Rodriguez (9:40 pm ET)
Tonight at Chase Field, all eyes will be on Gerrit Cole. Aside from the importance of the game on its own merits, it will be a crucial opportunity for the longtime Yankees ace to show whether he can still be counted upon as a frontline starter this postseason. After posting an exemplary 3.11 ERA in his first 16 starts back from Tommy John surgery, he’s stumbled in his last four, allowing 15 runs in 22.2 innings. Most concerning has been his battle with the long ball, having allowed seven in his last two starts. With Cam Schlittler, Max Fried, and Carlos Rodón firing on all cylinders, a strong outing tonight will help reassure the Yankees that Cole’s recent struggles are just a blip and that he belongs squarely in their playoff rotation.
Cole will face a fellow veteran hurler who’s in the midst of a career year. At the age of 33, Eduardo Rodríguez made his first All-Star team this year and has been a rock for the D-Backs, going 15-6 with a 2.62 ERA that quietly ranks fourth in the NL. Opponents are hitting below the Mendoza line against his heater and are slugging just .335 against his changeup, his top complementary pitch. The latter weapon has been particularly effective against righties, against whom the southpaw has fared batter this year than his fellow lefties. Rodríguez labored his last time out, allowing six runs in 5.1 innings, though only three were earned as the D-Backs committed two costly errors in the fifth.
Saturday: Cam Schlittler vs. Brandon Pfaadt (8:10 pm ET)
When the conversation turns from Cy Young to MVP, you’ve entered rarified air. If the season ended today, Cam Schlittler’s 2026 would rank second in Yankees history in WHIP (0.904) and eighth in ERA (1.95). He’s already seventh in strikeouts (228) and could easily crack the top three with two more representative outings. The last time Schlittler allowed more than a run in one of his starts was on August 3rd. He allowed no runs and one hit in his last outing as he ran roughshod over the Mets. At this point in the season, Schlittler is as close to a sure thing as it gets.
He’s lined up to face Brandon Pfaadt. A hero of the D-Backs’ run to the World Series in 2023, Pfaadt has struggled to establish himself in the intervening years. After spending some time in the bullpen and in the minors this year, he rejoined the rotation on June 30 and has been lights out ever since, going 7-2 with a 2.83 ERA over 12 starts. That ERA was as low as 2.38 before his last outing, a six-run implosion in which he allowed 10 hits to the Rangers in 6.1 innings. Pfaadt doesn’t get many strikeouts but also walks few, relying on soft contact generated by his six-pitch mix to work through lineups.
Thursday: Will Warren vs. Corbin Burnes (4:10 pm ET)
Will Warren may have nine lives. In mid-August, it looked like his days in the rotation were numbered with Rodón scheduled to return from injury. Instead, with Fried and Ryan Weathers landing on the shelf, the 27-year-old got a reprieve. He’s made the most of it, going 2-0 with a 1.38 ERA in his last five outings (four starts) while allowing just two home runs. While he’s unlikely to crack the playoff rotation barring injury, Warren has helped reassert himself as a valuable asset in the bullpen this postseason and in the rotation going forward.
The D-Backs are scheduled to hand the ball to Corbin Burnes. After signing a six-year megadeal with Arizona before the 2025 season, he made only 11 starts before missing a year-plus to Tommy John surgery. Burnes has made just two outings since his return and has looked rusty. His last time out, the former Cy Young Award winner allowed five runs in 4.2 innings to the Marlins. He threw just 75 pitches in that start as he continues to ramp up, and it’s unclear if he’ll be permitted to shoulder a full starter’s workload this time out.
